summary: Sirach 26 begins by praising a good and faithful wife as a gift that brings joy, peace, and honor to a household. It then turns sharply to fears, slander, jealousy, sexual suspicion, and warnings about women the speaker views as dangerous or uncontrolled. After verses 19–27, which are blank in the World English Bible, the chapter closes with grief over social reversal and a warning about the moral difficulty of trade.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows Sirach applying wisdom instruction to household life, reputation, sexuality, and commerce. It also exposes the ancient male household setting of the book, where praise of women and patriarchal suspicion stand close together.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; the Greek form was translated by his unnamed grandson in Egypt.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews who wanted to live according to the law.
context.date: Hebrew composition in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; Greek translation after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple, Torah study, household order, public reputation, and marketplace conduct all treated as settings for wisdom.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction in poetic maxims and vivid comparisons; this chapter is a sequence of household and social sayings, with verses 19–27 left blank in the World English Bible.

outline.heading: The blessing of a good wife
outline.note: A good and faithful wife is described as joy, peace, and a great gift, while a good heart brightens life whether one is rich or poor.

outline.heading: Fears worse than death
outline.note: The teacher names public slander, mob assembly, and false accusation as dangers that deeply trouble him.

outline.heading: Warnings about jealousy and shame
outline.note: The chapter uses harsh images for jealousy, drunkenness, sexual misconduct, and a headstrong daughter; readers should notice the ancient male household viewpoint rather than treating it as neutral psychology.

outline.heading: Beauty, restraint, and household order
outline.note: The praise returns to grace, knowledge, silence, modesty, self-control, beauty, and the well-organized home.

outline.heading: Absent Verses in This Edition
outline.note: The World English Bible leaves verses 19–27 blank. Sirach survives in shorter and longer textual forms, with differences in included lines and numbering.

outline.heading: Grief over reversal and sin
outline.note: The speaker grieves over a poor warrior, wise people despised, and someone turning back from righteousness to sin.

outline.heading: The danger of dishonest trade
outline.note: The chapter closes by saying merchants and retailers face particular difficulty avoiding wrongdoing and sin.

keyVerses.text: Happy is the husband of a good wife. The number of his days will be doubled.
keyVerses.why: This opening line states the chapter’s first major claim: a good wife is portrayed as a source of deep blessing for her husband.

keyVerses.text: A good wife is a great gift. She will be given to those who fear the Lord.
keyVerses.why: The verse connects household blessing with the book’s wider concern for the fear of the Lord.

keyVerses.text: A modest woman is grace upon grace. There are no scales that can weigh the value of a self-controlled soul.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the second praise section, where modesty and self-control are valued beyond ordinary measurement.

keyVerses.text: It is difficult for a merchant to keep himself from wrong doing, and for a retailer to be acquitted of sin.
keyVerses.why: The final verse shifts from household counsel to marketplace ethics, another ordinary setting where Sirach tests wisdom.

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin by praising a wife in terms of the husband’s happiness?
questions.answer: The chapter is written from the viewpoint of an ancient male wisdom teacher addressing household life. It describes a good wife by the benefit she brings to her husband: joy, peace, long life, and honor. That viewpoint should be named plainly; the text praises women, but it does so within a patriarchal household frame.

questions.question: What does “fear the Lord” mean here?
questions.answer: In this verse, a good wife is said to be given to those who fear the Lord. The broader book uses this phrase for a life of reverent allegiance to God, shown in wisdom, discipline, and faithful conduct. The chapter itself does not define the phrase, so the safest point here is that household blessing is being placed inside Sirach’s larger religious wisdom frame.

questions.question: Why does verse 4 mention being rich or poor?
questions.answer: Verse 4 widens the opening beyond marriage to the condition of the heart. Whether someone is rich or poor, the chapter says a good heart makes the face cheerful. In context, it keeps the first praise section from being only about status or money.

questions.question: Why are slander, mob assembly, and false accusation called worse than death?
questions.answer: The verse presents public disgrace and communal danger as terrifying threats. It does not give a legal case or a story; it names fears that could destroy a person’s standing and safety. The language is deliberately intense, showing how seriously Sirach treats reputation and public accusation.

questions.question: How should a reader handle the harsh statements about women in verses 6-12?
questions.answer: These verses reflect patriarchal suspicion and speak about women through the concerns of a male household world: jealousy, shame, sexual control, and family reputation. The text depicts those concerns; it should not be flattened into timeless neutral advice or used as permission to police or demean women. Readers differ on how to apply such material, but responsible reading first names the power arrangement the sayings assume.

questions.question: What does the image of a “chafing yoke” and a “scorpion” do?
questions.answer: Verse 7 uses painful physical images to describe the danger the speaker associates with a wicked woman. A yoke that chafes wounds the one under it, and a scorpion is dangerous to grasp. The point is not a calm description of all women, but a sharp warning image within the chapter’s negative section.

questions.question: Why are verses 13-18 so different in tone from verses 6-12?
questions.answer: The chapter alternates between warning and praise. After severe warnings about jealousy, drunkenness, and sexual misconduct, it returns to a positive portrait of a wife marked by grace, knowledge, silence, modesty, self-control, beauty, and steadiness. The contrast is part of the chapter’s teaching style, but it also intensifies the idealized expectations placed on women.

questions.question: Why are verses 19-27 blank in this chapter?
questions.answer: The World English Bible leaves verses 19–27 blank. Sirach survives in different textual forms, and editions can differ in wording and verse numbering. Other editions may include additional lines or number the passage differently.

questions.question: Why does the chapter end by warning merchants and retailers?
questions.answer: The ending shifts from household life to public and economic life. Verse 29 says it is difficult for a merchant or retailer to avoid wrongdoing and sin, suggesting that trade brings recurring moral pressure. The chapter does not condemn commerce itself; it warns that ordinary business can become a place where wisdom is tested.

glossary.def: The chapter’s positive figure for a wife whose presence brings joy, peace, and honor to her household.
A wife described as giving joy to her husband and helping him fulfill his years in peace.
A public charge the speaker fears, grouped with slander and mob assembly as more grievous than death.
A person marked by restraint; verse 15 says its value cannot be weighed on scales.
A trader used in the final verse as an example of someone who faces difficulty avoiding wrongdoing.
